# Tar archive extracted without a safe extraction filter (Python)

`qualor:python/tar-extraction` · Security hotspot · Severity: Medium · [CWE-22](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A01:2025 Broken Access Control](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/), [A01:2021 Broken Access Control](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/)

> **Security hotspot.** This rule asks for a review: it marks code that is often safe and
> sometimes not, and a person decides which. A hotspot never fails the quality gate.

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Tar archives extracted without a safe extraction filter, for a person to check where the
archive comes from:

- `TarFile.extractall()` and `TarFile.extract()` with no `filter=` argument (unless the
  archive's `extraction_filter` was set to a safe filter first), with `filter=None`, or with the
  `fully_trusted` filter: `filter="fully_trusted"`, `tarfile.fully_trusted_filter`, or a filter
  that returns each member unchanged (`lambda member, path: member`, also set as
  `extraction_filter`);
- the Python documentation's fallbacks for versions without filters, which extract unfiltered
  there: a call without a filter in the `else` branch of `if hasattr(tarfile, "data_filter")`,
  and `extraction_filter = getattr(tarfile, "data_filter", lambda member, path: member)`;
- `shutil.unpack_archive()` with no filter or the same unsafe ones, unless the archive is a zip
  (`format="zip"` or a literal `.zip` file name).

It follows archives opened with `tarfile.open()`, `TarFile()` and its class methods, in the same
function or module, in a `with` statement, as a parameter typed `tarfile.TarFile`, or kept on
`self` by `__init__`. Any other filter is accepted: `"data"`, `"tar"`, `tarfile.data_filter`,
`tarfile.tar_filter`, or a filter function of your own. So is a check of each member before
extracting it: an `if` in a loop over the archive, on the member or a path computed from it, that
raises, returns or exits (or, for `extract()` inside the loop, skips the member with `continue`).
A check on a character prefix stays reported, since `/srv/data-evil` starts with `/srv/data`:
`startswith(root)` without a separator at the end, and `os.path.commonprefix()`. Compare with
`os.path.commonpath()`, or with `root + os.sep`.
Other archive libraries (`zipfile`, `py7zr`) are not reported, and test code is not scanned.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
A tar archive can describe files with absolute names (`/etc/cron.d/job`), names with `..`
components, and symbolic or hard links that point anywhere; a later member can then write
through such a link. Without a filter, Python 3.13 and older create all of that as stored, so an
archive from a user, a download or another system can overwrite files outside the target
directory (CWE-22), and can create device files or set-user-ID bits. Python 3.14 extracts with
the `data` filter by default, but code that runs on older versions, or that passes
`fully_trusted`, still trusts the archive completely. The Python documentation recommends
passing `filter="data"` explicitly for that reason, and warns that even the filters do not
make untrusted archives entirely safe.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** a downloaded release is extracted with whatever the archive says.

```python
import tarfile


def install_release(archive_path, dest):
    with tarfile.open(archive_path) as tar:
        tar.extractall(dest)
```

**Compliant:** the `data` filter strips leading slashes from names, refuses members that would
land outside `dest` and links that point outside it or to absolute paths, and refuses device files.

```python
import tarfile


def install_release(archive_path, dest):
    with tarfile.open(archive_path) as tar:
        tar.extractall(dest, filter="data")
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- If the archive is one your program builds or has verified itself, mark the finding as reviewed.
- Otherwise pass `filter="data"` (or `filter=tarfile.data_filter`) to `extractall()`,
  `extract()` and `shutil.unpack_archive()`; use `"tar"` only when you need UNIX features such
  as links inside the directory and file modes.
- To support Pythons without filters, follow the docs' "Supporting older Python versions"
  section, and refuse to extract (rather than fall back to unfiltered extraction) where you can.
- For untrusted archives, also follow the docs' "Hints for further verification": extract into
  a new temporary directory, refuse links you do not need, and limit the number and size of the
  files.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- `tarfile`
- `shutil`

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- An archive passed in as a parameter without a type, or returned by a helper or another module,
  is not followed.
- Options passed as a dict (`extractall(dest, **opts)`) are not read and not reported.
- Any check of the member that raises, returns or exits counts, even one that does not look at
  its path (`if not member.isfile(): continue` lets a regular file named `../x` through), one
  made by a helper function in the condition, and one nested in another condition. A check
  on a literal or f-string prefix without a separator (`startswith("/srv/data")`,
  `startswith(f"{root}")`) also counts, although a sibling directory passes it.
- Skipping members by a name prefix held in a variable (`if member.name.startswith(SKIP):
  continue`) before `extract()` in the loop looks like a character-prefix check, so the call is
  reported even next to a real check.
- Checks of the member names before extraction do not stop links: a symbolic or hard link
  member can point outside the directory and a later member be written through it. Only the
  `data` filter refuses such links.
- A named filter function that returns each member unchanged is not reported.
- A prefix that ends in a separator but is kept in a variable (`prefix = root + os.sep`) is
  taken for a character prefix, so its check is reported.
- Checks the rule does not read are reported: a check in a helper function, a `members=`
  generator that yields only checked members, an `if` with more than one statement before its
  exit, and an exit by `break`.
- A default filter set once on the `TarFile` class for the whole program is not seen.
- `shutil.unpack_archive()` cannot tell a zip from a tar when the file name is a variable, so a
  zip extracted that way is reported.
- Test code (`test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, `conftest.py`, `tests.py`, `tests/`, `test/`) is not
  scanned.
<!-- end: known-limits -->
